title: No. 15 — The Insufficiency of the Present Confederation to Preserve the Union (Hamilton)
paragraphs: In the preceding papers, my fellow citizens, I have tried to show clearly and convincingly how important the Union is to your political safety and happiness. I have laid out the many dangers you would face if you allowed the sacred bond uniting the people of America to be cut or dissolved by ambition, greed, jealousy, or misrepresentation. In what follows, the truths I want to drive home will be confirmed further by facts and arguments not yet considered. If the road you still have to travel sometimes seems tedious, remember that you are seeking information on the most momentous subject that can occupy a free people. The territory you must cover is vast, and the difficulties of the journey have been needlessly multiplied by the mazes that sophistry has built across the path. My aim is to remove the obstacles before you as efficiently as possible, without sacrificing usefulness for speed.

Following the plan I set out for this discussion, the next point to examine is the "insufficiency of the present Confederation to preserve the Union." It might be asked why we need to argue for a position that no one disputes, that all classes of people accept in their understanding and feelings, and that even the opponents of the new Constitution essentially concede. However much they may differ in other respects, friends and opponents of the Constitution generally agree on this much: there are serious flaws in our national system, and something must be done to rescue us from approaching anarchy. The facts supporting this view are no longer matters of speculation. They have forced themselves on the attention of the people at large. They have at last extracted, even from those whose mistaken policy did most to bring us to the brink, a reluctant admission of the defects in our federal government—defects long pointed out and lamented by intelligent friends of the Union.

We have, in truth, reached almost the last stage of national humiliation. There is hardly anything that can wound the pride or degrade the character of an independent nation that we are not enduring. Are we bound by every honorable tie to keep our engagements? Those engagements are constantly and shamelessly violated. Do we owe debts to foreigners and to our own citizens, contracted in a time of grave danger to preserve our political existence? They remain without proper or adequate provision for repayment. Do we have valuable territories and important posts in the hands of a foreign power that, by express stipulation, should long ago have been surrendered? They are still held, to the harm of our interests and our rights. Are we able to resent or repel this aggression? We have neither troops, nor treasury, nor government.(1) Are we even able to protest with dignity? The just charges against our own faith with regard to the same treaty would have to be removed first. Are we entitled by nature and treaty to share freely in the navigation of the Mississippi? Spain bars us from it. Is public credit an indispensable resource in time of public danger? We seem to have abandoned that cause as desperate and beyond rescue. Is commerce important to national wealth? Ours is at the lowest point of decline. Does respectability in the eyes of foreign powers safeguard us from foreign encroachments? The weakness of our government even prevents foreign nations from negotiating with us. Our ambassadors abroad are mere puppets of pretended sovereignty. Is a violent and unnatural drop in the value of land a symptom of national distress? The price of improved land in most parts of the country is much lower than the supply of unsold land alone could explain. It can only be fully explained by the alarming lack of private and public confidence prevailing among all ranks, which directly tends to depreciate property of every kind. Is private credit the friend and patron of industry? The most useful kind—lending and borrowing—has been reduced to the narrowest limits, and this stems even more from a sense of insecurity than from a shortage of money. To shorten this catalog, which can give neither pleasure nor instruction, we may ask in general: what sign of national disorder, poverty, and insignificance could befall a community as blessed with natural advantages as we are, that does not appear on the dark list of our public misfortunes?

This is the gloomy situation to which we have been led by the very maxims and councils that would now deter us from adopting the proposed Constitution. Not content with bringing us to the edge of a precipice, they seem determined to plunge us into the abyss below. Here, my countrymen, driven by every motive that should move an enlightened people, let us make a firm stand for our safety, our peace, our dignity, our reputation. Let us at last break the fatal spell that has too long lured us from the paths of happiness and prosperity.

It is true that facts too stubborn to resist have produced a kind of general assent to the abstract proposition that there are serious flaws in our national system. But the usefulness of that concession by the old opponents of federal measures is destroyed by their stubborn opposition to the only kind of remedy that can succeed. They admit that the government of the United States lacks energy, but they oppose giving it the powers needed to supply that energy. They still seem to aim at incompatible things—an increase of federal authority without any decrease of State authority, sovereignty in the Union and complete independence in the members. In short, they still seem to cling, with blind devotion, to the political monster of an imperium in imperio, a government within a government. This makes it necessary to lay out the principal defects of the Confederation, in order to show that the evils we suffer do not come from minor or partial imperfections but from fundamental errors in the structure of the building. They cannot be fixed except by altering the first principles and main pillars of the fabric.

The great and radical vice in the construction of the existing Confederation is the principle of LEGISLATION for STATES or GOVERNMENTS in their CORPORATE or COLLECTIVE capacities, as opposed to the INDIVIDUALS who make them up. This principle does not run through every power delegated to the Union, but it pervades and governs those on which the effectiveness of the rest depends. Except for the rule of apportionment, the United States has unlimited discretion to make requisitions for men and money. But it has no authority to raise either through regulations that reach the individual citizens of America. The result is that, although in theory their resolutions on these matters are laws constitutionally binding on the members of the Union, in practice they are mere recommendations that the States observe or ignore at will.

It is a strange instance of the human mind's caprice that, after all the warnings experience has given us on this point, there should still be people who object to the new Constitution for departing from a principle that has proven the bane of the old. This is a principle plainly incompatible with the very idea of GOVERNMENT—a principle that, if it is to be carried out at all, must replace the mild influence of the magistracy with the violent and bloody work of the sword.

There is nothing absurd or impractical in the idea of a league or alliance between independent nations for certain defined purposes precisely stated in a treaty—regulating all the details of time, place, circumstance, and quantity, leaving nothing to future discretion, and depending for its execution on the good faith of the parties. Compacts of this kind exist among all civilized nations, subject to the usual ups and downs of peace and war, of observance and non-observance, as the interests or passions of the contracting powers dictate. Early in the present century there was an epidemic enthusiasm in Europe for this kind of compact, from which the politicians of the day fondly hoped for benefits that never came. To establish the balance of power and the peace of that part of the world, every resource of negotiation was used. Triple and quadruple alliances were formed, but they were scarcely formed before they were broken. They gave mankind an instructive but painful lesson in how little reliance can be placed on treaties whose only sanction is good faith and which set general considerations of peace and justice against the impulse of any immediate interest or passion.

If the particular States in this country wish to stand in a similar relation to one another and drop the project of general DISCRETIONARY SUPERINTENDENCE, the scheme would indeed be harmful and would bring upon us all the evils enumerated under the first head. But it would at least have the merit of being consistent and practical. Abandoning all aims of confederate government, it would reduce us to a simple alliance offensive and defensive. It would place us in a position to be alternate friends and enemies of one another, as our mutual jealousies and rivalries—stoked by the intrigues of foreign nations—dictated.

But if we are unwilling to be placed in that perilous position, if we still adhere to the design of a national government—or, what is the same thing, of a superintending power directed by a common council—then we must resolve to incorporate into our plan the ingredients that distinguish a league from a government. We must extend the authority of the Union to the persons of the citizens, who are the only proper objects of government.

Government implies the power to make laws. Essential to the idea of a law is that it be backed by a sanction—that is, a penalty or punishment for disobedience. If no penalty is attached to disobedience, the resolutions or commands that pretend to be laws will in fact amount to nothing more than advice or recommendation. This penalty, whatever it is, can only be imposed in two ways: by the courts and ministers of justice, or by military force; by the COERCION of the magistracy, or by the COERCION of arms. The first method clearly applies only to individuals. The second must be used against bodies politic—communities or States. There is plainly no court process by which the observance of laws can ultimately be enforced against a State. Sentences may be pronounced against States for violating their duty, but those sentences can only be carried out by the sword. In an association where general authority is confined to the collective bodies that compose it, every violation of the laws must mean a state of war, and military execution becomes the only instrument of civil obedience. Such a state of things certainly cannot be called government, and no prudent man would commit his happiness to it.

There was a time when we were told that breaches by the States of federal regulations were not to be expected—that a sense of common interest would govern the conduct of the respective members and produce full compliance with all the constitutional requisitions of the Union. That language now seems as wild as much of what we hear today from the same quarter will seem once experience, the best oracle of wisdom, has given us further lessons. Such language always betrayed ignorance of the true springs of human conduct and ignored the original reasons for establishing civil power. Why was government instituted at all? Because the passions of men will not yield to the dictates of reason and justice without restraint. Has it ever been found that bodies of men act with more uprightness or greater disinterestedness than individuals? The opposite has been observed by every careful student of human conduct, and the inference rests on obvious reasons. Concern for reputation has less force when the disgrace of a bad action is divided among many than when it falls on one person alone. A spirit of faction, which tends to mix its poison into the deliberations of all bodies of men, will often drive the people in those bodies into improprieties and excesses they would blush to commit as private individuals.

Beyond all this, there is in the nature of sovereign power an impatience of control, which makes those who exercise it look with hostility on any external attempt to restrain or direct its operations. From this spirit it follows that in every political association formed to unite a number of lesser sovereignties in a common interest, there is a kind of eccentric tendency in the subordinate bodies—a constant effort in each to fly off from the common center. This tendency is not hard to explain. It originates in the love of power. Power that is controlled or limited is almost always the rival and enemy of the power that controls or limits it. This simple proposition shows how little reason there is to expect that the people running the affairs of the particular members of a confederacy will at all times be ready, with perfect good humor and unbiased regard for the public good, to carry out the resolutions or decrees of the general authority. The opposite is the natural result of human nature.

Therefore, if the measures of the Confederacy cannot be carried out without the intervention of the particular State administrations, there is little chance they will be carried out at all. The rulers of the respective members, whether they have a constitutional right to do so or not, will judge the propriety of the measures themselves. They will weigh how the proposal fits their immediate interests or aims, and the momentary conveniences or inconveniences of adopting it. All of this will be done in a spirit of self-interested and suspicious scrutiny, without the knowledge of national circumstances and reasons of state that sound judgment requires, and with such a strong bias toward local objects that it can hardly fail to mislead the decision. The same process must be repeated in every member of the body, and the execution of plans framed by the councils of the whole will always depend on the discretion of the ill-informed and prejudiced opinion of every part. Anyone familiar with the proceedings of popular assemblies—who has seen how hard it often is to bring them to harmonious resolutions on important points without outside pressure—will easily grasp how impossible it must be to induce a number of such assemblies, deliberating at a distance from one another, at different times, and under different impressions, to cooperate long in the same views and pursuits.

In our case, the agreement of thirteen distinct sovereign wills is required, under the Confederation, for the complete execution of every important measure of the Union. The result has been what should have been foreseen. The measures of the Union have not been carried out. The delinquencies of the States have, step by step, grown to such an extreme that they have stopped all the wheels of national government and brought them to a dead halt. Congress at this point barely has the means to keep up the forms of administration until the States can agree on a more substantial replacement for the present shadow of a federal government. Things did not reach this desperate extremity all at once. The causes I have specified at first produced only unequal and disproportionate degrees of compliance with the Union's requisitions. The greater deficiencies of some States gave the complying or least delinquent States both an excuse of example and a temptation of self-interest. Why should we do more proportionally than those traveling with us in the same political voyage? Why should we agree to bear more than our fair share of the common burden? These suggestions human selfishness could not resist, and even speculative men looking ahead to remote consequences could not, without hesitation, oppose them. Each State, yielding to the persuasive voice of immediate interest or convenience, has successively withdrawn its support, until the frail and tottering edifice seems ready to fall on our heads and crush us beneath its ruins.
